candidates.headline: Fable 5 and Mythos 5 return after a 19-day export-control shutdown — the outage that taught enterprises AI is now infrastructure, not a feature
candidates.summary: The US Commerce Department lifted the export-control order (imposed 12 June after an Amazon researcher demonstrated a safeguard-bypass in Fable 5) and Anthropic restored Fable 5 globally on 1 July, with Mythos 5 returning to approved US organisations. Because Anthropic could not verify user nationality in real time, it had suspended access for everyone for 19 days rather than risk breaching the rule — a self-imposed global outage of a frontier model. Commentary frames the lesson as single-vendor AI-dependency risk: teams that had wired Fable/Mythos into production had no fallback.
candidates.so_what: A concrete, non-hypothetical case that a frontier model can vanish for 19 days on a regulatory trigger — forcing a model-portability / multi-provider fallback conversation for anyone with agents or LLM calls in production.
candidates.notes: Strong Wider-engineering-landscape / Operating-at-scale candidate; passes the 'would it matter at Mozilla?' cross-industry test (any org with the model in production felt it). Regulatory but scope-conditional bar is cleared — implications cross-industry, not confined to one regulated entity class. In-window restoration (1-2 Jul). Frame as vendor/model-concentration risk, not US-policy commentary. Clean non-AWS lead alternative for Operating at scale, and a non-fintech anchor option.

in_practice.headline: Airbnb's build-vs-buy on observability: why they left vendor tooling, what the first migration got wrong, and owning the interaction layer
in_practice.source_name: The Airbnb Tech Blog (Callum Jones & Rong Hu)
in_practice.summary: Named operators Callum Jones and Rong Hu describe Airbnb's journey from vendor observability tools to an in-house platform: vendors billed on data volume while more data didn't cut MTTD/MTTR, and the org lacked control over how data was used. Migration v1 failed by tackling the hardest service first and faithfully porting flawed queries. The pivots: start with tractable high-leverage services, translate the intent of a query not one-to-one, and invest in developer experience (authoring tools, alerting) over just swapping backends. The leadership lesson: own the interaction layer (frontend, authoring, workflows), not necessarily the backend.
in_practice.so_what: A named operator's build-vs-buy journey framed as a leadership decision — exactly the technical-leadership theme the next In Practice season should pull from, and non-AI.
in_practice.notes: STRONG fit for the pivot the season note calls for: technical-leadership theme (build-vs-buy / architectural decision as a manager), named operator at a real org, journey-not-framework, implication-level (the reader won't tune the queries but learns what the org got wrong and why). NON-AI — helps long-form variety. RECENCY: published 17 Mar 2026 — outside the 30-day fresh window, so use under the evergreen-eligibility clause with the 'a classic worth revisiting' sub-label, or hold. Do NOT also use Airbnb as Outside In in the same issue (deconflict).

in_practice.headline: Duolingo's incident-command lessons from search-and-rescue: the hardest incidents aren't complex, they're chaotic
in_practice.summary: Maggie Hewitt, a Duolingo engineer and volunteer with Allegheny Mountain Rescue, draws parallels between managing search-and-rescue incidents and long-running engineering crises: the hardest incidents are chaotic, not complex, and demand formal command structure, shared documentation as a single source of truth, explicit task ownership so the coordinator doesn't become a bottleneck, and pre-established artefacts you build before the chaos. Incident command is a distinct skill from technical problem-solving.
in_practice.so_what: A named operator's transferable playbook for leading a long, chaotic incident — a crisis-leadership / ways-of-working craft piece the reader can apply without running the systems themselves, and non-AI.
in_practice.notes: Named operator, first-person, journey-not-framework, implication-level — strong In Practice fit and NON-AI.
